entities.name: Theodor von Sitten
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Theodore of Octodurum, the first historically attested bishop of Octodurum (modern Martigny, Switzerland), stands as a foundational figure in the Christianization of the Western Alps during the late 4th century CE. Operating within the Roman province of Alpes Poeninae, his episcopacy marks a critical juncture in the transition from paganism to an organized Christian ecclesiastical structure in a strategically important alpine region. As the enduring patron saint of Valais and of the Walser people, Theodore's legacy transcends his initial historical role, embedding his figure deeply within the cultural and religious identity of the Swiss Alps.

The core of Theodore's historical significance lies in his leadership of the nascent Christian community in Octodurum, a key Roman administrative and commercial hub at the confluence of major alpine passes. While specific details of his life and actions are sparse, traditional accounts and early ecclesiastical records confirm his status as the inaugural bishop, thereby establishing a formal episcopal see that would persist for centuries, eventually relocating to Sion. His period, culminating in his death around 400 CE, coincides with the final decades of a unified Roman Empire and the increasing institutionalization of Christianity following the Edict of Milan (313 CE) and the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), making his work crucial for the consolidation of Christian influence in peripheral territories.
